Social Studies.title: Social studies week: compare urban, suburban, and rural places
Social Studies.subject: Social Studies
Social Studies.contentMarkdown:
**Verified NYC course:** **Urban, Suburban, and Rural Communities** is one of four Grade 2 Passport units under **My Community and Other Communities**. The public course page establishes the topic but does not expose every student reading; use the assigned Passport guide/workbook for the class's exact images and questions. [NYC Grade 2 Passport](https://sites.google.com/schools.nyc.gov/social-studies-and-civics/resources-by-grade/elementary/2nd-grade).

![Conceptual comparison: dense city buildings, a lower-density neighborhood, and open land](images/grade-02/social-studies/g02-social-community-types.png)

*Concept art only: left to right, common urban, suburban, and rural clues. It is not a map, census classification, or portrait of real neighborhoods; communities can include mixed features.*

#### Learn it in plain English

**Urban, suburban, and rural** are words used to compare communities. Urban places often have more buildings close together. Suburban places often have neighborhoods with buildings farther apart than in a dense city. Rural places often have more open land and fewer buildings close together. These are clues for comparing a map or picture, not strict rules: a community can have a busy center, quiet blocks, parks, and open land all together.

Communities can have different services, homes, roads, parks, and ways to travel. Use a source to find out what is actually present. A picture may show a bus or houses, but it cannot tell how often the bus comes, who lives there, what people do for work, or whether everyone has the same experience. Avoid statements such as “all rural people live on farms” or “everyone in a city uses the same transportation.”

The class image above is an **illustration**, not an actual New York neighborhood. It gives three visual examples to sort: dense tall buildings on the left, lower-density homes in the middle, and widely separated homes/open land on the right. For real-place claims, switch to the actual Passport reading, photographs, or maps and name the source.

#### Five study sessions

| Session | 45–60-minute lesson and work | End check |
|---|---|---|
| 1 — Notice and describe | Look at the concept image and list only visible details: building height/spacing, roads, trees, and open space. Read the Passport definition or captions when available and record the source. | Descriptions begin “I can see…” and do not guess jobs, income, or culture. |
| 2 — Learn the three words | Use the actual Passport lesson's examples. Match urban, suburban, and rural to the source's pictures or community profiles. Compare the visible clues with the concept image. | Each label is supported by the source, and mixed examples may be described as mixed. |
| 3 — Compare resources and travel | From the assigned source, find which services, transport options, or open spaces it actually names/shows. Record “shown,” “not shown,” or “not sure”; do not fill missing details with guesses. | The student can name the exact picture/map/text that supports each fact. |
| 4 — Compare two communities | Use two real Passport examples or one source example and a verified local map/photo. Record one similarity and two differences. Mark whether each point is from an image, a map, or a written source. | A comparison names sources and uses visible or written evidence. |
| 5 — Write a community comparison | Complete the practice set. Write a short paragraph comparing two communities, including a careful label, evidence, and one thing the source does not tell. | The paragraph avoids “all people…” statements and distinguishes fact from inference. |

#### Practice set — new source-reading questions, not Passport workbook questions

Questions 1–4 use the concept image above. Questions 5–12 require an actual Passport page, teacher-approved photograph, or map; if that source is unavailable, write “source needed” instead of guessing.

1. Which part of the concept image shows buildings closest together?
2. Which part shows the most open land between homes?
3. Name one visible difference between the left and middle parts of the image.
4. Can the concept image prove what jobs people have or how they travel every day? Why?
5. From the Passport source, choose one urban example. Copy its name and list two features the source shows.
6. Choose one suburban example in the source. What evidence supports that label?
7. Choose one rural example in the source. What evidence supports that label?
8. Find one resource or service shown/named in each of two examples. Which source shows it?
9. Compare how people travel in two source examples. If the source does not say, what should you write?
10. Write one similarity between two communities using evidence from both.
11. Correct this claim: “Everyone in a rural community lives on a farm.”
12. Write a three-sentence comparison: label each community, give one supported difference, and name one detail the source does not tell.

questions.prompt: After trying the practice above, briefly note that you are ready to compare your work with the guide’s checked responses.

visuals.placement: Social studies, compare urban, suburban, and rural communities; beside the Grade 2 Passport week.

Social Studies.answerKeyMarkdown:
#### Checked answer and review guide

1. **Left side**, where the tall buildings are close together.
2. **Right side**, where homes are spread apart and more open land is visible.
3. Example: the left has many tall buildings close together; the middle has lower homes with more space. Accept any accurate visible comparison.
4. **No.** The picture shows buildings and land arrangement, not people's jobs or daily travel.
5–9. Answers depend on the actual Passport page/map/photo. Check the copied place name and evidence against that source. If it does not show the requested fact, “not shown/source needed” is correct.
10. Answers vary. The same feature must be visible or stated in both sources; name both.
11. Not everyone in a rural community lives on a farm. Use the source to describe its settlement pattern and resources without claiming all residents do the same thing.
12. Answers vary. Credit accurate, source-backed labels and comparison, plus an honest limit. Do not accept unsupported details about residents.

**Mastery check:** the learner uses urban/suburban/rural as comparison words, describes evidence before labeling, names the source, recognizes mixed community features, and avoids guessing about residents or their lives.

Social Studies.title: Social studies week: rights, rules, and responsibilities
Social Studies.subject: Social Studies
Social Studies.contentMarkdown:
![Blank chart for right, responsibility, rule, and decision-maker, with a space to ask who should be heard](images/grade-02/social-studies/g02-social-rights-rules-organizer.png)

Fill the chart with examples from the assigned source or a real classroom/community situation. It is an organizer, not a source of civics facts.

**Verified course and grade expectations:** NYC Passport Grade 2 includes **Rights, Rules, and Responsibilities**. The New York State Grade 2 framework calls for identifying community political leaders (such as a mayor), the governor, and the president and their leadership roles; it also asks students to identify rights and responsibilities in the classroom, school, and community. P.S. 139 names Passport as its social studies resource; P.S. 179's current unit calendar is not public. Use the actual Passport source/workbook for its specific reading and task. [NYC Grade 2 Passport](https://sites.google.com/schools.nyc.gov/social-studies-and-civics/resources-by-grade/elementary/2nd-grade); [P.S. 139 academic program](https://www.ps139.org/curriculum__academic_programs); [NYS K–8 Social Studies Framework, Grade 2 civic participation practice](https://www.nysed.gov/sites/default/files/programs/standards-instruction/ss-framework-k-8a2.pdf).

#### Learn it in plain English

A **rule** says what people in a group or place are expected to do. A **right** is a protection or freedom people should have under the relevant rules or laws. A **responsibility** is an action people are expected to take. They connect: one person's choices can affect another person's ability to learn, feel safe, or take part. A classroom rule and a city law are not the same thing; name the place and decision-maker before describing a rule.

Examples for practice: “Take turns using shared supplies” is a possible classroom rule. “Return the shared materials” is a responsibility in that classroom example. A right or protection should be tied to the actual school or community source being studied; do not invent a legal promise from a classroom poster. The Passport workbook may give the lesson's exact cases, and access may require an NYCPS account.

The Grade 2 framework names three government leaders: a **mayor** for a community/city, a **governor** for a state, and a **president** for the country. The framework asks children to identify these leaders and their responsibilities. This lesson uses those offices, not the current officeholders, so the material stays useful when elections change. A student should match a concern to a level only when the source explains who handles it.

When a rule affects a group, ask: What problem is the rule trying to solve? Who is affected? What might be fair to different people? Who has the job or authority to decide? Listening to classmates is good civic practice, but a class vote is not the same process as every city, state, or national decision.

#### Five study sessions

| Session | 45–60-minute lesson and work | End check |
|---|---|---|
| 1 — Read the real course source | Read the teacher-assigned Passport page or workbook for this unit. Record its title, page, people/group, problem, and any exact rule or right it names. If the book is not available, use the framework facts above and mark source-dependent answers “need the workbook.” | No plot, rule, or rights detail is added unless the source says it. |
| 2 — Sort rights, rules, and responsibilities | Use examples from the source first. Then make a separate classroom example card. Sort each statement and explain the reason; leave uncertain legal claims blank for an adult/source check. | The learner distinguishes a rule from a responsibility and ties a right to a source. |
| 3 — Match leaders to levels | Make a three-column chart: community/city—mayor; state—governor; country—president. Add responsibilities only from the source or an official page. Do not add current leader names to the lasting student guide. | Each office is matched to its level; the learner does not mix city, state, and national roles. |
| 4 — Fair rule case | Read the case below about shared classroom materials. Identify the problem, who is affected, a possible rule, and the responsibility the rule asks of students. Consider whether the rule treats students fairly and ask who should approve it. | Rule and responsibility fit the described classroom case; the learner names who should be heard. |
| 5 — Explain and act | Complete the practice set. Write a short proposal for one classroom or community concern. Give one reason, name who is affected, and identify the source/adult who can confirm the right decision-maker. | The proposal uses evidence and does not claim a student has authority to change a city or school rule alone. |

**Practice case (new example, not a Passport excerpt):** students share markers for a group poster. Some students cannot finish because one person keeps all the markers. Possible class rule: return markers to the shared box after each use. Possible responsibility: use a marker, then return it so other group members can take a turn. The example illustrates reasoning; it is not a statement of a school policy.

#### Practice set — new questions, not school/workbook questions

1. Match each office to its level: mayor, governor, president; community/city, state, country.
2. In the shared-marker case, what problem does the possible rule address?
3. In the same case, name the possible rule and a student responsibility that fits it.
4. Is “return the shared markers after using them” a rule or a responsibility? Explain one valid way to describe it.
5. Why should the guide use office titles instead of writing the current mayor's, governor's, and president's names into the lasting lesson?
6. A student says a classroom poster proves a city law. What source should the student check before making that claim?
7. A rule affects students who use classroom supplies differently. Name two questions to ask before calling the rule fair.
8. Does listening to student ideas mean students alone decide every school or city rule? Explain.
9. Find one right or responsibility in the actual Passport source. Copy a short phrase in your own notes, write the page, and explain its meaning in simple words.
10. Name a classroom issue and propose one rule that addresses it. Say who should be heard before the rule is adopted.
11. A community concern is outside a student's classroom. Which Grade 2 leader titles can the framework help identify? What extra source is needed to know who handles that exact concern?
12. Write one sentence that distinguishes a right, a rule, and a responsibility in the shared-marker example.

questions.prompt: After trying the practice above, briefly note that you are ready to compare your work with the guide’s checked responses.

visuals.alt: Blank chart sorts a source's examples into rights, responsibilities, rules, and decision-makers.
visuals.placement: Social studies, rights, rules, responsibilities, and participation.

Social Studies.answerKeyMarkdown:
#### Checked answer and review guide

1. **Mayor—community/city; governor—state; president—country.**
2. Some group members cannot use the shared materials because one person keeps them.
3. Possible rule: return markers to the shared box after use. Responsibility: return the marker so others can use it. Accept an equivalent fair rule.
4. It can be worded as a **rule** for the class and also describes a **responsibility** students take on. The student's explanation should say which view they mean.
5. Officeholders can change, while the roles remain. Check a current official source before adding names to dated material.
6. Check the **actual city law or official city source**; a classroom poster does not prove a city law.
7. Answers vary. Good questions include: Who needs the supplies? Can everyone get a turn? Does the rule create a barrier for anyone? Is the rule applied the same way?
8. **No.** Listening is participation; the school or government has its own decision process and responsible officials.
9. Answers depend on the actual Passport source. Accept only a source-matched phrase/page and a simple explanation that keeps the meaning.
10. Answers vary. The rule must address the named issue; include people affected and someone responsible for approving it (for a classroom, the teacher/school process).
11. The framework identifies the **mayor, governor, and president** as community/state/country leaders. Check an official source for the exact agency or official responsible for the particular issue.
12. Example: “A right is a protection people have; the class rule says markers go back in the shared box; each student's responsibility is to return a marker after using it.”

**Mastery check:** the learner uses the real course source for rights claims, separates rules from responsibilities, matches the three leader offices to their levels, and explains who is affected and who should be heard before a rule is made.

Social Studies.title: Social studies week: community resources and interdependence — New York City water
Social Studies.subject: Social Studies
Social Studies.contentMarkdown:
![Blank organizer linking source places, a community water system, and people served, with space for limits](images/grade-02/social-studies/g02-social-resource-connections.png)

**End-of-week review:** Without looking, name what the DEP overview reports for reservoirs, controlled lakes, and approximate daily supply; then check each number on the official page. **Answers:** 19 reservoirs, 3 controlled lakes, about 1 billion gallons per day. Explain in one sentence why these citywide facts do not tell how much one student uses. **Check:** per-person use would need different data. Finish with a source caption and have an adult verify every number and map label before the poster is shared.

**Extended evidence and writing practice:** (7) Why can a city depend on places outside its borders? **Check:** people and systems may connect a city's needs with resources and workers in a larger region; use DEP's map/overview as NYC-water evidence. (8) Draw three boxes: “source region,” “water system,” and “people served.” Add arrows with a fact from the official source. **Check:** do not draw an exact route from reservoir to tap unless DEP shows it. (9) Write one question that needs an adult or official source. **Possible:** “How is water tested before it reaches homes?” (10) Why does a resource map need a key? **Symbols need meanings so readers can understand what is shown.** (11) Name one way people can care for a shared resource. **Possible:** follow official conservation guidance; cite the local source if naming a specific rule. (12) Write a paragraph with one DEP fact, one explanation of interdependence, and one question still open. **Check:** distinguish what DEP says from your idea. A partner should trace each fact to the DEP page/map and mark unsupported arrows. This builds the Passport idea of communities relying on resources beyond their own boundaries without asking a Grade 2 student to memorize the whole water system.

**Why this belongs:** the NYC Grade 2 Passport overview says students study community resources and interdependence within and across communities. This week uses one real, documented example: NYC’s drinking-water system. NYC DEP says its system provides about one billion gallons of drinking water each day to city residents and includes 19 reservoirs and three controlled lakes across a watershed that reaches into the Hudson Valley and Catskill Mountains. Those figures describe the citywide system, not a student’s personal water use. [NYC Grade 2 Passport overview](https://sites.google.com/schools.nyc.gov/social-studies-and-civics/resources-by-grade/elementary/2nd-grade) · [NYC DEP Water Supply](https://www.nyc.gov/site/dep/water/water-supply.page) · [official NYC water-supply system map (PDF)](https://www.nyc.gov/assets/dep/downloads/pdf/water/drinking-water/water-supply/nyc-water-supply-system.pdf).

**Authentic visual:** [Open NYC DEP’s official water-supply system map (PDF)](https://www.nyc.gov/assets/dep/downloads/pdf/water/drinking-water/water-supply/nyc-water-supply-system.pdf). It labels the watershed, reservoirs, city, and water infrastructure.

#### Source reading: where New York City's water system reaches

NYC's Department of Environmental Protection (DEP) reports that its water-supply system provides about **one billion gallons of drinking water each day** to the city's **8.5 million residents**. DEP also reports that the system sends about **110 million gallons a day** to about **one million people** in four nearby counties: Westchester, Putnam, Orange, and Ulster.

DEP says the system includes **19 reservoirs and three controlled lakes**. Its watershed covers about **2,000 square miles** in parts of the Hudson Valley and Catskill Mountains. Some areas are as far as **125 miles north of New York City**. DEP groups the supply into the Catskill, Delaware, and Croton systems. These are citywide system facts from DEP; they do not tell how much water one family uses or which pipe brings water to one apartment. [NYC DEP, Water Supply](https://www.nyc.gov/site/dep/water/water-supply.page).

**Learn it simply:** a **resource** is something people use to meet a need. A **watershed** is land where rain and other water drain toward streams, rivers, lakes, or reservoirs. A **reservoir** is a place where water is stored. A **system** is a group of connected parts that work together. NYC's map shows the city's water system reaches beyond the five boroughs. That is an example of **interdependence**: people and places rely on one another. The map is an overview of a large system, so a Grade 2 learner should use its title, key, and labels with an adult rather than try to read every symbol. [U.S. EPA, “Wetlands and Watersheds”](https://www.epa.gov/sites/default/files/2021-01/documents/wetlands_and_watersheds.pdf).

**Read the map carefully:** first find the map title and legend. Point to New York City. Then locate one labeled reservoir and compare its position with the city. Say only what the map shows: the labeled places and the broader system. A line on a regional map does not prove the exact pipe route to a particular building. Use a written source for facts the map cannot show, such as how much water one household uses.

1. **Day 1 — Read the city source:** with an adult, read the DEP overview. Find the daily amount, the number of reservoirs, and the regions where DEP says the watershed is located. Copy each fact with its source heading.
2. **Day 2 — Read the real map:** find New York City, read the legend, and locate one labeled reservoir. Describe where that place is compared with the city. Make a two-column chart: “the map shows” / “the map does not show.” Do not claim it traces water to a home.
3. **Day 3 — Sort facts and inferences:** sort six cards made from the DEP reading into “DEP says” and “my explanation.” Examples: “DEP lists 19 reservoirs” is a source fact; “the system connects people and places” is an explanation based on the source facts. Check every number against DEP and add a heading or page clue.
4. **Day 4 — Explain interdependence:** draw and label a three-part chain: watershed and water sources → city water-supply system → people served. Write two sentences: one says what DEP reports; the other explains why places and people beyond the city matter. Mark any part the map does not establish.
5. **Day 5 — Make a source-based poster:** use the genuine DEP map (or draw only a simple labeled locator, not a copy of the infrastructure map). Add a title, three checked labels, one source fact, an interdependence sentence, and a “map limit” note. Read the poster aloud and verify each fact and label with an adult.

**Practice questions — use the source reading and map:**

1. How many reservoirs does DEP list?
2. How many controlled lakes?
3. About how much drinking water does the system provide to NYC residents each day?
4. About how many NYC residents does DEP say this serves?
5. What additional amount and population does DEP report for nearby counties?
6. Name the four nearby counties DEP lists.
7. Name the three water-supply systems.
8. About how large is the watershed?
9. In which broad regions is it located?
10. How far north of NYC can some watershed areas be?
11. Does DEP say that every person in NYC uses the same amount? Explain.
12. Does the regional map show the exact pipe route to one apartment? Explain.
13. Why is this an example of interdependence?
14. Give one fact from DEP and one explanation in your own words. Label which is which.
15. Name one thing the map shows and one thing it cannot prove.

**Checked answer key:**

1. **19 reservoirs.**
2. **Three controlled lakes.**
3. **About one billion gallons.**
4. **8.5 million people.**
5. **About 110 million gallons each day for about one million people.**
6. **Westchester, Putnam, Orange, and Ulster.**
7. **Catskill, Delaware, and Croton.**
8. **About 2,000 square miles.**
9. **Parts of the Hudson Valley and Catskill Mountains.**
10. **As far as 125 miles north of New York City.**
11. **No.** Citywide gallons and population do not show how much each person or family uses.
12. **No.** The map is an overview, not a map of a household's pipe route.
13. People in the city rely on a system that includes water sources and infrastructure across a wider region. Accept similar wording that names both the city and the broader region.
14. Answers vary. The DEP fact must match the source; the explanation must be labeled as the student's thinking, not as a DEP quotation.
15. The map shows labeled places and the regional system. It cannot prove one household's route or a family's water use.

**Visual note:** reuse the official DEP map above; do not generate a replacement map or treat it as a street-level map. The existing Grade 2 community-types visual is a generic comparison aid, not a map of actual NYC neighborhoods.

visuals.alt: Blank flow organizer helps students explain how a resource source, community system, and people connect.
visuals.placement: Social studies, community resources/interdependence; accompany the real NYC DEP system map.

Science.title: Science week: how seeds can travel with animals
Science.subject: Science
Science.contentMarkdown:
**Model-limit reflection:** Finish these two lines after the investigation: “Our model included ___.” “A real habitat may differ because ___.” **Check:** name an actual model feature and a real-world factor the model leaves out; do not claim to know what happened in a real forest from a classroom model. Keep the model drawing, measurement table, and explanation together so another student can see how the claim follows from results.

**Explain the result to a younger learner:** Point to one value in the class table, say what it measures, and explain whether it supports the model question. **Check:** include the number, unit, and trial; do not say a single test proves what happens in nature. If two trials differ, report both rather than choosing the result you prefer.

**Extended investigation practice:** (6) Make a table for the animal-dispersal model. Use the exact categories in the teacher's assigned page, including the number of droppings and the number of seeds that reach suitable growing places when the lesson asks for them. **Check:** categories match the source and each number comes from the class or assigned source data. (7) In a separate wind-seed investigation, record each teacher-selected seed design, each measured distance, and the unit. **Check:** do not combine animal-model counts with wind-model distances. (8) What should stay the same when comparing two seed designs for travel distance? **Check:** keep the start point, measuring method, and release method the same unless the assigned investigation changes one on purpose. (9) If one model sends a seed marker farther, does that prove a real bird will carry that seed that far? **No;** it is evidence about that model and setup. (10) Draw a seed path and label the start, mover, landing place, and one condition needed for growth. **Check:** landing does not guarantee sprouting. (11) Write one observation and one prediction. **Check:** an observation reports an actual record; a prediction says what may happen and can be tested. (12) What evidence from a real habitat could help test the class idea? **Possible:** carefully collected field observations or published research on real seeds, animals, wind, and seedlings. Do not disturb wildlife or plants.

**Verified curriculum anchor:** P.S. 139 lists Amplify Science. Amplify's Grade 2 **Plant and Animal Relationships** unit is tied to New York's Grade 2 expectation 2-LS2-2: make a simple model that imitates how an animal can help spread seeds or pollinate plants. Its published unit guide explicitly calls the Bengal Tiger Reserve case a **fictional** scenario. In that scenario, students investigate why no new chalta trees are growing and test ideas with models and data. This verifies the published curriculum example; it does not prove P.S. 179 uses Amplify, or that either class is on this unit now. [Amplify Grade 2 unit guide](https://amplify.com/wp-content/uploads/2021/10/ASCA_UnitGuide_G2_PAR_101821.pdf); [Amplify Grade 2 overview](https://sciencek8.amplify.com/grades-k-5/); [P.S. 139 program list](https://www.ps139.org/curriculum__academic_programs); [New York State P–12 Science Learning Standards](https://www.nysed.gov/sites/default/files/programs/curriculum-instruction/p-12-science-learning-standards.pdf).

![Generated generic example of an animal moving a seed away from its parent plant; a seed's landing does not show that it will sprout](images/grade-02/science/g02-science-seed-dispersal.png)

*Generated generic example, not a photograph or the exact Amplify class model. This picture shows a bird, while the unit guide's fictional chalta-tree example uses elephants. The image's intended labels are not visible in the delivered PNG, so use the nearby text for the labels. A seed landing does not show that it will sprout.*

**Learn it simply:** plants make seeds. A seed can grow only if it reaches a place with conditions it needs. Some seeds move away from the parent plant with help from animals. In the Amplify lesson, children model and measure seed movement; the class uses its own recorded results as evidence. Do not claim a certain seed traveled farthest until you have the actual measurement table.

#### Source reading: the unit's fictional chalta-tree investigation

The published Amplify unit guide says its Bengal Tiger Reserve story is fictional. In the story, chalta trees make seeds, but students are asked to explain why new chalta trees are not growing in one part of the reserve. The guide has students first learn that seeds need water and sunlight to sprout and grow. It also explains that a new plant needs enough space for its roots and leaves.

The guide's explanation for this story connects seeds to animals. In the fictional case, elephants eat chalta fruit, move to another place, and leave seeds in their droppings. The guide says a fence built in **1996** keeps elephants from entering that part of the reserve, so they can no longer move chalta seeds there. This is the unit's model explanation—not a report about a real reserve or proof about real elephants.

The same guide gives other examples of seed movement in the story world: wind can carry seeds from sal trees and red silk trees. This helps students compare ways seeds can move. An animal, wind, or water can carry a seed, but arriving somewhere is not the same as growing there. A seed still needs suitable conditions. The full unit has students use models and investigations to gather evidence; for an actual class, use the teacher's assigned materials and measured results rather than this summary as a substitute for the student book. [Amplify Grade 2 unit guide, *Plant and Animal Relationships*](https://amplify.com/wp-content/uploads/2021/10/ASCA_UnitGuide_G2_PAR_101821.pdf).

**Source check:** Label each statement in your notes as one of these: (A) a fact about the fictional Amplify story, (B) an observation from your group's model, or (C) a claim about a real habitat. The unit guide can support A. Your own table can support B. Neither alone proves C.

**Five sessions:** This is a focused study week built from activities in Amplify's published Lessons 2.5, 3.2–3.6, and 4.1–4.3. It is not a claim about either student's current school calendar or a replacement for the assigned unit pages.

1. **Read the case and label the evidence:** read the unit guide's question and this source summary. Mark the reserve as fictional. In the teacher's assigned data, find what students compare about seed needs. Record one source fact and one question the evidence has not answered yet.
2. **Model animal movement:** use the actual Amplify activity/materials if the teacher has them. Draw the source's sequence: animal eats fruit, moves, and leaves seeds in another location. Label which parts the model represents and which details are simplified.
3. **Count and analyze:** follow the assigned model directions to record how many droppings and seeds reach places where seeds may get what they need. Copy actual results into a table. Check the category labels and count before explaining a pattern; do not substitute made-up data.

Science.title: Science week: test and compare material properties
Science.subject: Science
Science.contentMarkdown:
![Blank investigation chart for material, tested property, prediction, same test steps, result, and evidence](images/grade-02/science/g02-science-material-test-organizer.png)

Use one row for each material, mixture, or test the class actually performs. Keep the observation column blank until the test is done.

**Verified unit:** P.S. 139 names Amplify Science. Its public program page does not confirm the exact edition/calendar. Amplify's California Grade 2 **Properties of Materials** guide describes a 22-lesson unit in which students act as “glue engineers” and design a school glue with desired properties. This week is a five-session sampler of that published content, not a claim that P.S. 139 or P.S. 179 teaches it this week. [P.S. 139 program list](https://www.ps139.org/curriculum__academic_programs); [Amplify Grade 2 unit guide](https://amplify.com/wp-content/uploads/2021/10/ASCA_UnitGuide_G2_POM_101821.pdf); [Amplify teacher-provided materials list](https://amplify.com/wp-content/uploads/2021/07/ASCA-MaterialsList-TeacherProvided-G2.pdf).

#### What the real unit guide covers

The unit's starting question is how to make a sticky glue. Students read *What If Rain Boots Were Made of Paper?*, observe and test two mystery glues, and collect evidence to decide whether the glues are the same or different. They read *Handbook of Interesting Ingredients* and test possible glue ingredients for stickiness. The guide names ingredients such as flour, water, and cornstarch; it does not supply one result that every classroom must get. Students graph their own sticky-test results, plan and make a glue mixture, and later add strength as another design goal. They read *Jess Makes Hair Gel*, revise recipes after testing, and present which final mixture best meets the design goals.

The guide also includes a heating/cooling chapter. It says water can return to its earlier properties after heating and cooling, while a heated cornstarch-and-water mixture can have different properties after returning to room temperature. Heating equipment and mixtures belong only in the teacher's approved lesson with adult handling. Do not heat materials at home or taste classroom mixtures. Use the publisher's full lesson directions for the exact recipe, test setup, and safety steps.

#### Learn it in plain English

A **material** is what an object is made from. A **property** is something you can observe or test about it. A rain boot needs material properties suited to keeping feet dry; the Amplify student book uses the “What If Rain Boots Were Made of Paper?” question to introduce how material choices fit a purpose. In this unit, students study properties such as stickiness and strength because they are designing glue.

A **mixture** combines ingredients. The final mixture's properties depend on its ingredients and how they are combined. The publisher guide gives flour, water, and cornstarch as possible glue ingredients. It explains that different recipes can have different properties. It does **not** tell every class that one recipe will always be the stickiest; students collect evidence from the tests they actually run.

Engineers use a design cycle: understand the problem, name the goal, choose ingredients, make a design, test it, record evidence, and revise. If the glue must be sticky and strong, both properties matter. A mixture that meets one goal but not the other may need a new recipe. When making a claim, use the real class data: “Our mixture ____. The test showed ____. This evidence suggests ____.”

#### Five study sessions

| Session | 45–60-minute lesson and work | End check |
|---|---|---|
| 1 — Materials have properties | Read the assigned *What If Rain Boots Were Made of Paper?* pages. Make a table of object, material, visible/testable property, and purpose. Connect the reading to the glue-engineering challenge. | Each property is observable or testable; do not guess a material's performance without a source or test. |
| 2 — Mystery glues and evidence | Follow the actual Amplify mystery-glue activity with teacher-provided samples. Record what the class observes and the exact test used. Use the evidence to argue whether the two glues seem the same or different. | Claims name an observed property and the test; no results are supplied in advance. |
| 3 — Test ingredients | Read the assigned pages of *Handbook of Interesting Ingredients*. With the teacher, follow the official ingredient observation/sticky-test directions. Record ingredient, prediction, test steps, actual result, and evidence. | The procedure matches the class directions, and the prediction is separate from the result. |
| 4 — Graph and design | Graph the class's real test data. Use the graph to decide which ingredients may help the sticky-glue goal. Follow teacher directions to make a first mixture; do not change an ingredient amount without approval. | The design choice points to actual bars/data and states one limit. |
| 5 — Add a goal and revise | Read the assigned *Jess Makes Hair Gel* or design-cycle section. Discuss how the unit adds strength to stickiness. Compare actual test evidence, suggest a revision, and write a short design argument for the mixture that best meets the class goals. | The claim addresses both goals and cites test results; if data are missing, mark “test needed.” |

#### Practice set — new questions based on the publisher guide

1. What job do students take on in the Amplify unit, and what are they trying to design?
2. Name two student books listed in the unit guide.
3. The guide names flour, water, and cornstarch as possible ingredients. Does it give one sticky-test result that must occur in every classroom?
4. What is one property the unit tests before it adds strength as a design goal?
5. Why does the unit have students observe two mystery glues before deciding whether they are the same?
6. What should a student write in the prediction column before a glue test?
7. After a test, which column should contain what the student actually saw or measured?
8. Why do students graph their own sticky-test results?
9. The unit later adds strength to stickiness. Why might a recipe need another test or revision?
10. According to the guide, what can happen to a cornstarch-and-water mixture after heating and returning to room temperature? Do not run this test yourself.
11. A student writes, “Mixture A is the best glue,” but gives no test data. What evidence should the student add?
12. Which mixture was stickiest in your class's actual results? If no test table is available, what is the honest answer?

3. **No.** The guide has students test and graph their classroom results; the result depends on the tested recipes and setup.

Science.title: Science week: how water can change land
Science.subject: Science
Science.contentMarkdown:
**Verified unit:** P.S. 139 names Amplify Science. The publisher's Grade 2 *Changing Landforms* guide describes a fictional Oceanside Recreation Center cliff that appears to recede, and has students use sand samples, water/chalk and other models, maps, and readings to investigate erosion. The publicly named P.S. 139 program does not confirm which edition or classroom calendar the teacher uses. This five-session plan draws from the published California unit guide; it is a study supplement, not a claim about the exact lessons taught at P.S. 139 or P.S. 179. The full publisher unit has 22 lessons, so this is not the whole unit. [Amplify Grade 2 *Changing Landforms* unit guide](https://amplify.com/pdf/uploads/2021/10/ASCA_UnitGuide_G2_CL_101821.pdf); [P.S. 139 program list](https://www.ps139.org/curriculum__academic_programs).

![Before-and-after model of water carrying loose sediment away from a land edge](images/grade-02/science/g02-science-erosion-before-after.png)

*Generated model, not a real coastline or Amplify image. Left shows one possible starting shape; right shows one possible change. It does not measure erosion or predict how fast a real cliff changes.*

#### What the real unit guide says

Amplify's guide gives students the role of geologists. Its starting question is how the edge of the fictional cliff came to be so close to a flagpole. The chapter on water says water hit the cliff, causing tiny pieces to break off and move away. Students investigate sand and find that it is made of tiny pieces of rock; they use a hard-candy model to visualize how small pieces can form; then they investigate water changing landforms with a chalk model and read the student book *What's Stronger? How Water Causes Erosion*. A later lesson considers the scale of erosion in a chalk model and investigates pumice. The guide emphasizes that many small changes can build into a large change over time.

Use the publisher's assigned reading and lesson steps for exact student-book content. The summary above is a paraphrase of the guide, not copied text from the student books. Its figure of a receding cliff is fictional; do not present it as a measured New York coastline.

#### Learn it in plain English

A **landform** is a shape of land, such as a cliff, hill, or valley. **Erosion** is a process in which moving water or wind causes pieces of rock or soil to break off and move. Sand is made of small rock pieces. A cliff can look almost the same from one day to the next even while many small changes add up over a long time. Some loose materials can erode faster than solid rock; the material and the water/wind conditions matter.

Models help answer questions that are hard to watch directly. Chalk, sand, hard candy, pumice, or pom-poms in the publisher guide are model materials, not exact copies of a real cliff. If a model changes quickly, that does not prove a real cliff changes at the same speed. Record what happened to the model, then explain what it helps you think about and what it cannot show.

#### Five study sessions

| Session | 45–60-minute lesson and work | End check |
|---|---|---|
| 1 — Notice the landform | Read the assigned pages from *Handbook of Land and Water* and examine the unit's cliff photos/maps with the teacher. Record what changed in the flagpole-to-edge evidence, then list questions the pictures cannot answer by themselves. | Separate a visible change from a guess about its cause. |
| 2 — Examine sand and model pieces | Follow the actual guide's sand-sample lesson: observe and compare samples by visible features, make a simple sample card, and connect sand grains to pieces of rock using the assigned reading. If using the hard-candy model from the guide, follow adult directions and do not eat materials used in a model. | A description gives observed size/shape/color; it does not claim all sand is identical. |
| 3 — Model water erosion | With the teacher, follow the class's approved chalk/water setup from the unit. Draw the chalk before, observe the water/model interaction, and record what pieces or marks changed. Do not substitute an unapproved experiment for the publisher protocol. | State only what was observed in this trial. |
| 4 — Read and diagram | Read *What's Stronger? How Water Causes Erosion* as assigned. Create a labeled diagram showing the source-supported sequence: water contacts land, small pieces break off, and pieces move away. Add arrows with words so the reader knows what each arrow means. | Each diagram step is supported by the reading/model, not added as a guessed event. |
| 5 — Think about scale | Revisit the chalk model and the guide's scale-of-erosion work. Compare a small model change with the larger cliff question; discuss why many small changes can add up and why model speed is not a real-world rate. Write one claim, one observation, and one model limit. | The explanation does not predict an exact date or rate for a real cliff. |

#### Practice set — new questions based on the actual unit guide

1. What is the fictional landform in the Amplify unit, and what nearby object helps show its edge changed?
2. According to the publisher's chapter 2 summary, what does water do to the cliff material?
3. What are sand grains made from, according to the unit guide?
4. Why does the guide use models such as chalk or hard candy instead of waiting to watch a real cliff for years?
5. Put these steps in order: small pieces move away; water hits the land; small pieces break off.
6. A student sees a mark on a chalk model after the water activity. Is that an observation or an explanation? Give one example of each.
7. The model changes in a few minutes. Can the student say a real cliff will change by the same amount in a few minutes? Why?
8. Name two model materials listed in the guide's investigations.
9. How can many tiny changes create one large change over time?
10. The later unit asks how a nearby cliff made of loose material could erode quickly. What material comparison does the guide emphasize?
11. Write one claim about the class model, one observation from the actual trial, and one limit. Use your own class data for the observation.
12. Name one question about a real cliff that this classroom model cannot answer.

Science.answerKeyMarkdown:
#### Checked answer key

1. A **cliff**; the **flagpole** is the nearby object used to compare the cliff edge over time.
2. Water hits it; **tiny pieces break off and move away**.
3. Sand is made of **tiny pieces of rock**.
4. A classroom model lets students examine change and evidence in a short lesson. It does not replace long-term measurements of an actual cliff.
5. **Water hits the land → small pieces break off → small pieces move away.**
6. “There are new marks/loose pieces” is an **observation** if seen in the trial. “Water caused the change” is an **explanation** supported by the setup and evidence.
7. **No.** A model is not the same material, size, or time scale as a real cliff; it cannot establish a real-world rate.
8. Any two from the guide: **sand, hard candy, chalk, pumice, pom-poms**.
9. Many changes too small to notice one at a time can accumulate until the landform's shape changes noticeably.
10. The guide contrasts **loose materials such as clay and dirt**, which can erode more quickly, with **solid rock**.
11. Answers depend on the actual trial. Accept a claim that matches the setup, an observation copied from the student's data, and a limit such as “our chalk is not a whole cliff.” Do not accept invented observations.
12. Answers vary. Examples: how quickly a real local cliff is changing, what its layers are made of, or whether it is safe; those need real measurements or a qualified source, not only the classroom model.

**Mastery check:** the student uses the actual reading/model, orders the erosion steps, separates observation from explanation, and states why a classroom model cannot give a real cliff's exact rate or safety condition.

### P.S. 139 — school-published program

P.S. 139 identifies **Illustrative Mathematics** as its primary math curriculum. Its school-published Grade 2 annual map lists: **Adding, Subtracting, and Working with Data; Adding and Subtraction within 100; Measuring Length; Addition and Subtraction on the Number Line; Numbers to 1,000; Geometry, Time, and Money; Adding and Subtracting within 1,000; Equal Groups;** and **Putting it All Together**. P.S. 179 has not publicly identified a current Grade 2 math textbook in the sources located. [P.S. 139 Curriculum Maps by Month](https://www.ps139.org/curriculum_maps_by_month).

### Actual curriculum example (P.S. 139 program resource)

The Illustrative Mathematics Grade 2, Unit 1 family resource gives this task: **“Andre read 45 pages of his book last night. Priya read 20 fewer pages of her book than Andre. How many pages did Priya read? Explain or show your reasoning.”** The official curriculum solution is **25 pages**: subtract 20 from 45. One valid visual is a tape diagram with a 45-page bar split into 20 pages plus 25 pages; the 25-page segment is Priya's amount. The solution guide itself gives 25 pages and a diagram-based subtraction explanation.

The same source's bar graph uses students' favorite pets. Its official answer notes that 10 students chose dogs, fish received 2 more votes than lizards, and 11 students chose cats or fish together. These are the actual graph facts in that curriculum activity, not invented data. [Open Up Resources / Illustrative Mathematics, Grade 2 Unit 1 family materials and solutions](https://cms-assets.illustrativemathematics.org/icxvbqzzuiz4fnwuwzqj07de3mfb) (CC BY-NC 2024, pp. 3–4).

- **Place value and operations:** hundreds, tens, and ones; read/write/compare numbers; add and subtract within the grade-level range; explain strategies.

- **Measurement and data:** standard units, money, time, length, picture/bar graphs, and solving one- and two-step situations.
- **Geometry and fractions:** describe and sort shapes; partition shapes into equal shares.

For source-authentic additional math questions, use the [NYSED released Grades 3–8 math tests](https://www.nysed.gov/state-assessment/past-grades-3-8-tests) for older grades; NYSED does not publish a Grade 2 state math test.
